steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper proposing a unifying generator loss function for GANs. It should review VanillaGAN and its issues, the related dual-objective and divergence-based GANs (RényiGAN, f-GAN, alpha-GAN), then present our L_alpha-GAN and its Jensen-type divergence result, and finish with the paper outline.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- GANs: background and how they are trained
- Variants and training issues (DCGAN, mode collapse, vanishing gradients)
- VanillaGAN objective and the JSD result; RényiGAN analogue
- f-GAN

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- GANs
  - Goodfellow et al., 2014 (cite); applications: media generation (cite), image restoration (cite), data privacy (cite)
  - generate synthetic data resembling real data, unknown distribution {P_{\mathbf{x}}}; train so {P_{\mathbf{g}}} approximates it
  - low-dim random noise -> generator network G; real + generated -> discriminator D, scores between 0 and 1 (close to 1 = real)
  - minimax game: minimize generator's loss, maximize discriminator's loss
- Variants / issues
  - DCGAN (cite): same losses as VanillaGAN (original GAN), adds convolutional nets, extract visual features for images
  - more stable than baseline, but mode collapse: generator learns a few images fool D, only generates those
  - VanillaGAN: vanishing generator gradients; early on D not confident, assigns generated data values near zero -> objective near zero, small gradients, no learning
  - fix: non-saturating generator loss (cite original paper)
- VanillaGAN objective
  - negative sum of two Shannon cross-entropies; min by G, max by D
  - optimal fixed D -> minimize Jensen-Shannon divergence (JSD) between real and generated distributions (cite)
  - analogous for RényiGANs (cite): dual-objective, distinct D/G losses; canonical D loss (as in original paper), G loss with two Rényi cross-entropies -> minimize Jensen-Rényi divergence; extends VanillaGAN result
- f-GAN
  - Nowozin et al. (cite): class of losses parametrized by lower semicontinuous convex f
  - minimize f-divergence between true and generator distributions via minimax of Fenchel conjugate representation; D replaced by variational function estimating ratio of distributions
  - loss tedious to derive (Fenchel conjugate of f)
  - interpolates between VanillaGAN and HellingerGAN, among others (cite)
- alpha-GAN
  - presented in (cite): losses parameterized by \alpha>0, CPE loss between real label y\in\{0,1\} and predicted label \hat{y} in the unit interval
  - tuning \alpha as hyperparameter helps across datasets (different optimal \alpha)
  - further analyzed (cite), expanded (cite): dual-objective (\alpha_{D},\alpha_{G}) -GAN, distinct \alpha for D and G, aim training stability
  - \alpha_{D}=\alpha_{G}: reduces to minimizing Arimoto divergence (cite)
  - recovers several f-GANs: HellingerGAN, VanillaGAN, WassersteinGAN, Total Variation GAN (cite)
  - recent work unifying the three earlier papers (cite): one-to-one correspondence CPE-loss GANs <-> f-GANs with symmetric f-divergence (cite)
  - generalization + estimation error bounds; mitigate instability on synthetic Gaussian data, Celeb-A, LSUN Classroom
  - but no analogue of JSD / Jensen-Rényi results for VanillaGAN (cite) and RényiGAN (cite): no Jensen-type divergence
- Our contribution
  - unifying axiomatic framework for several generator losses; GAN optimization in terms of Jensen-type divergence
  - class of \alpha-parameterized CPE losses \mathcal{L}_{\alpha}, generalizes \alpha-loss (cite)
  - \mathcal{L}_{\alpha} -GAN: dual objective; G uses loss from class, D any canonical loss with same optimizer as VanillaGAN (cite)
  - regularity (convexity/concavity) conditions -> minimax equivalent to minimizing Jensen- f_{\alpha} -divergence; another extension of JSD besides Jensen-Rényi (cite); f_{\alpha} computed from \mathcal{L}_{\alpha}
  - recovers prior dual-objective equilibrium results
  - Jensen- f_{\alpha} -divergence: symmetric f-divergence class (Remark 1); convex f with restricted domain, interval from 0 to 2 (Remark 2); symmetry, finiteness
- Organization
  - Sec. 2 f-divergences, Jensen-f-divergence; Sec. 3 main result (Theorem 1), applies to known GANs (Lemmas 2 - 4); Sec. 4 experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10, Stacked MNIST; Sec. 5 conclusion

steps.text:
Generative adversarial networks (GANs) were first introduced by Goodfellow et al. in 2014, and they have many applications, for example media generation, image restoration and data privacy. The aim of GANs is to generate synthetic data that is very similar to the original real data, which has an (unknown) underlying distribution {P_{\mathbf{x}}}. The GAN is trained so that the distribution of the generated data, {P_{\mathbf{g}}}, approximates {P_{\mathbf{x}}} well. In more detail, low-dimensional random noise is given to a generator neural network G which produces synthetic data. Then the real data and the generated data are given to a discriminator neural network D which scores the data between 0 and 1, and a score close to 1 means the discriminator thinks the data is from the real dataset. The discriminator and the generator play a minimax game, where the aim is to minimize the generator's loss and to maximize the discriminator's loss.

Several variants of GAN have been proposed since then. Deep convolutional GAN (DCGAN) uses the same loss functions as VanillaGAN (the original GAN), and combines GANs with convolutional neural networks, which are helpful for image data because they extract visual features from the data. DCGANs are more stable than the baseline model, but they can suffer from mode collapse. Mode collapse happens when the generator learns that a few select images can easily fool the discriminator, and then the generator only generates those images. Another notable issue with VanillaGAN is that the gradients of the generator network tend to vanish. In the early stages of training the discriminator is not confident and it assigns values close to zero to the generated data. So the objective function tends to zero, which gives small gradients and the network does not learn. To mitigate this issue the original paper proposed a non-saturating generator loss function so that the gradients do not vanish early in training.

In the original (VanillaGAN) problem setup, the objective function is a negative sum of two Shannon cross-entropies and it is minimized by the generator and maximized by the discriminator. It is shown that if the discriminator is fixed to be optimal (i.e., it maximizes the objective function), then the minimax game of the GAN reduces to minimizing the Jensen-Shannon divergence (JSD) between the probability distributions of the real and the generated data. A similar result was proven for RényiGANs, which is a dual-objective GAN that uses distinct loss functions for the discriminator and the generator. Under a canonical discriminator loss function (as in the original paper) and a generator loss function written with two Rényi cross-entropies, it is shown that the RényiGAN optimization problem reduces to minimizing the Jensen-Rényi divergence, so this extends the result of VanillaGAN.

  - recovers several f-GANs: HellingerGAN, VanillaGAN, WassersteinGAN, Total Variation GAN (cite)
  - recent work unifying the three earlier papers (cite): one-to-one correspondence CPE-loss GANs <-> f-GANs with symmetric f-divergence (cite)
  - generalization + estimation error bounds; mitigate instability on synthetic Gaussian data, Celeb-A, LSUN Classroom
  - but no analogue of JSD / Jensen-Rényi results for VanillaGAN (cite) and RényiGAN (cite): no Jensen-type divergence
- Our contribution
  - unifying axiomatic framework for several generator losses; GAN optimization in terms of Jensen-type divergence
  - class of \alpha-parameterized CPE losses \mathcal{L}_{\alpha}, generalizes \alpha-loss (cite)
  - \mathcal{L}_{\alpha} -GAN: dual objective; G uses loss from class, D any canonical loss with same optimizer as VanillaGAN (cite)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Generative adversarial networks (GANs) were first introduced by Goodfellow et al. in 2014, and they have many applications, for example media generation, image restoration and data privacy. The aim of GANs is to generate synthetic data that is very similar to the original real data, which has an (unknown) underlying distribution {P_{\mathbf{x}}}. The GAN is trained so that the distribution of the generated data, {P_{\mathbf{g}}}, approximates {P_{\mathbf{x}}} well. In more detail, low-dimensional random noise is given to a generator neural network G which produces synthetic data. Then the real data and the generated data are given to a discriminator neural network D which scores the data between 0 and 1, and a score close to 1 means the discriminator thinks the data is from the real dataset. The discriminator and the generator play a minimax game, where the aim is to minimize the generator's loss and to maximize the discriminator's loss.

Several variants of GAN have been proposed since then. Deep convolutional GAN (DCGAN) uses the same loss functions as VanillaGAN (the original GAN), and combines GANs with convolutional neural networks, which are helpful for image data because they extract visual features from the data. DCGANs are more stable than the baseline model, but they can suffer from mode collapse. Mode collapse happens when the generator learns that a few select images can easily fool the discriminator, and then the generator only generates those images. Another notable issue with VanillaGAN is that the gradients of the generator network tend to vanish. In the early stages of training the discriminator is not confident and it assigns values close to zero to the generated data. So the objective function tends to zero, which gives small gradients and the network does not learn. To mitigate this issue the original paper proposed a non-saturating generator loss function so that the gradients do not vanish early in training.

In the original (VanillaGAN) problem setup, the objective function is a negative sum of two Shannon cross-entropies and it is minimized by the generator and maximized by the discriminator. It is shown that if the discriminator is fixed to be optimal (i.e., it maximizes the objective function), then the minimax game of the GAN reduces to minimizing the Jensen-Shannon divergence (JSD) between the probability distributions of the real and the generated data. A similar result was proven for RényiGANs, which is a dual-objective GAN that uses distinct loss functions for the discriminator and the generator. Under a canonical discriminator loss function (as in the original paper) and a generator loss function written with two Rényi cross-entropies, it is shown that the RényiGAN optimization problem reduces to minimizing the Jensen-Rényi divergence, so this extends the result of VanillaGAN.

Nowozin et al. generalized VanillaGAN with a class of loss functions parametrized by a lower semicontinuous convex function f, and called it f -GAN. The f -GAN problem is to minimize an f -divergence between the true data distribution and the generator distribution, and this is done through a minimax optimization of a Fenchel conjugate representation of the f -divergence. Here the role of the VanillaGAN discriminator (a binary classifier) is replaced by a variational function that estimates the ratio of the true data and generator distributions. Deriving the f -GAN loss function can be tedious, since you need to compute the Fenchel conjugate of f. It can be shown that f -GAN can interpolate between VanillaGAN and HellingerGAN, among others.

More recently \alpha -GAN was presented. The aim there is to derive a class of loss functions parameterized by \alpha>0, written in terms of a class probability estimation (CPE) loss between a real label y\in\{0,1\} and predicted label \hat{y} between 0 and 1. Being able to control \alpha as a hyperparameter is useful to apply one system to multiple datasets, since two datasets may be optimal for different \alpha values. This work was analyzed further and expanded with the dual-objective (\alpha_{D},\alpha_{G}) -GAN, which lets the generator and discriminator loss functions have a distinct \alpha parameter, with the aim of improving training stability. When \alpha_{D}=\alpha_{G}, the \alpha -GAN optimization reduces to minimizing an Arimoto divergence, as was derived originally. Note that \alpha -GAN can recover several f -GANs, for example HellingerGAN, VanillaGAN, WassersteinGAN and Total Variation GAN. Also, in their more recent work which unifies these papers, the authors establish a one-to-one correspondence, under some conditions, between GANs based on CPE loss (like \alpha -GANs) and f -GANs that use a symmetric f -divergence. They also prove various generalization and estimation error bounds for (\alpha_{D},\alpha_{G}) -GANs and show that they can mitigate training instability for synthetic Gaussian data and also the Celeb-A and LSUN Classroom image datasets. But the various (\alpha_{D},\alpha_{G}) -GAN equilibrium results do not give a result that is analogous to the JSD and Jensen-Rényi divergence minimization for the VanillaGAN and RényiGAN problems, respectively, since no Jensen-type divergence is involved.

The main objective of our work is a unifying approach that gives an axiomatic framework that covers several existing GAN generator loss functions, so that the GAN optimization can be simplified in terms of a Jensen-type divergence. Our framework classifies the set of \alpha -parameterized CPE-based loss functions \mathcal{L}_{\alpha}, and this generalizes the \alpha -loss function from earlier work. Then we propose \mathcal{L}_{\alpha} -GAN, which is a dual objective GAN that uses a function from this class for the generator, and uses any canonical discriminator loss function that has the same optimizer as VanillaGAN. We show that under some regularity (convexity/concavity) conditions on \mathcal{L}_{\alpha}, the minimax game played with these two loss functions is equivalent to minimizing a Jensen- f_{\alpha} -divergence. This is a Jensen-type divergence and another natural extension of the Jensen-Shannon divergence (besides the Jensen-Rényi divergence), and the generating function f_{\alpha} of the divergence is computed directly from the CPE loss function \mathcal{L}_{\alpha}. This result recovers various earlier dual-objective GAN equilibrium results, so they are unified under one parameterized generator loss function. The new Jensen- f_{\alpha} -divergence belongs to the class of symmetric f -divergences with different generating functions (see Remark 1). It is a useful measure of dissimilarity between distributions, because it requires a convex function f with a restricted domain given by the interval from 0 to 2 (see Remark 2), and in addition it is symmetric and finite.

The rest of the paper is organized like this. In Section 2 we review f -divergence measures and introduce the Jensen- f -divergence as an extension of the Jensen-Shannon divergence. In Section 3 we give our main result about the optimization of our unifying generator loss function (Theorem 1), and we show it can be applied to a large class of known GANs (Lemmas 2 - 4). In Section 4 we do experiments where we implement different manifestations of \mathcal{L}_{\alpha} -GAN on three datasets, MNIST, CIFAR-10 and Stacked MNIST. Finally we conclude the paper in Section 5.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Generative adversarial networks (GANs), first introduced by Goodfellow et al. in 2014 [1], have a variety of applications in media generation [2], image restoration [3], and data privacy [4]. GANs aim to generate synthetic data that closely resembles the original real data with (unknown) underlying distribution {P_{\mathbf{x}}}. The GAN is trained such that the distribution of the generated data, {P_{\mathbf{g}}}, approximates {P_{\mathbf{x}}} well. More specifically, low-dimensional random noise is fed to a generator neural network G to produce synthetic data. Real data and generated data are then given to a discriminator neural network D that scores the data between 0 and 1, with a score close to 1 meaning that the discriminator thinks the data belongs to the real dataset. The discriminator and generator play a minimax game, where the aim is to minimize the generator's loss and maximize the discriminator's loss.

Since their initial introduction, several variants of GAN have been proposed. Deep convolutional GAN (DCGAN) [5] uses the same loss functions as VanillaGAN (the original GAN) and combines GANs with convolutional neural networks, which are helpful when applying GANs to image data as they extract visual features from the data. DCGANs are more stable than the baseline model, but can suffer from mode collapse, which occurs when the generator learns that a select number of images can easily fool the discriminator, so that it only generates those images. Another notable issue with VanillaGAN is the tendency of the generator network's gradients to vanish. In the early stages of training, the discriminator lacks confidence and assigns generated data values close to zero. Therefore, the objective function tends to zero, resulting in small gradients and a lack of learning. To mitigate this issue, a non-saturating generator loss function was proposed in [1] so that gradients do not vanish early on in training.

In the original (VanillaGAN) problem setup, the objective function, expressed as a negative sum of two Shannon cross-entropies, is minimized by the generator and maximized by the discriminator. It is shown that if the discriminator is fixed to be optimal (i.e., as a maximizer of the objective function), the GAN's minimax game reduces to minimizing the Jensen-Shannon divergence (JSD) between the real and generated data's probability distributions [1]. An analogous result was proven in [6] for RényiGANs, a dual-objective GAN using distinct discriminator and generator loss functions. More specifically, under a canonical discriminator loss function (as in [1]) and a generator loss function expressed in terms of two Rényi cross-entropies, the RényiGAN optimization problem is shown to reduce to minimizing the Jensen-Rényi divergence, thus extending VanillaGAN's result.

Nowozin et al. generalized VanillaGAN by formulating a class of loss functions in [7] parametrized by a lower semicontinuous convex function f, devising f -GAN. More specifically, the f -GAN problem consists of minimizing an f -divergence between the true data distribution and the generator distribution via a minimax optimization of a Fenchel conjugate representation of the f -divergence, where the role of the VanillaGAN discriminator (as a binary classifier) is replaced by a variational function estimating the ratio of the true data and generator distributions. The f -GAN loss function can be tedious to derive, as it requires computing the Fenchel conjugate of f. It can be shown that f -GAN can interpolate between VanillaGAN and HellingerGAN, among others [7].

More recently, \alpha -GAN was presented in [8], with the aim of deriving a class of loss functions parameterized by \alpha>0, expressed in terms of a class probability estimation (CPE) loss between a real label y\in\{0,1\} and predicted label \hat{y}\in[0,1] [8]. Being able to control \alpha as a hyperparameter is beneficial for applying one system to multiple datasets, as two datasets may be optimal under different \alpha values. This work was further analyzed in [9] and expanded in [10] by introducing the dual-objective (\alpha_{D},\alpha_{G}) -GAN, which allows the generator and discriminator loss functions to have a distinct \alpha parameter in order to improve training stability. When \alpha_{D}=\alpha_{G}, the \alpha -GAN optimization reduces to minimizing an Arimoto divergence, as originally derived in [8]. Note that \alpha -GAN can recover several f -GANs, such as HellingerGAN, VanillaGAN, WassersteinGAN and Total Variation GAN [8]. Furthermore, in more recent work which unifies [8,9,10], the authors establish, under some conditions, a one-to-one correspondence between CPE loss based GANs (such as \alpha -GANs) and f -GANs that use a symmetric f -divergence; see [11]. They also prove various generalization and estimation error bounds for (\alpha_{D},\alpha_{G}) -GANs and show their ability to mitigate training instability for synthetic Gaussian data as well as the Celeb-A and LSUN Classroom image datasets. However, the various (\alpha_{D},\alpha_{G}) -GAN equilibrium results do not provide an analogue to the JSD and Jensen-Rényi divergence minimization for the VanillaGAN [1] and RényiGAN [6] problems, respectively, as no Jensen-type divergence is involved.

The main objective of our work is to present a unifying approach that provides an axiomatic framework encompassing several existing GAN generator loss functions, so that the GAN optimization can be simplified in terms of a Jensen-type divergence. In particular, our framework classifies the set of \alpha -parameterized CPE-based loss functions \mathcal{L}_{\alpha}, generalizing the \alpha -loss function in [8,9,10,11]. We then propose \mathcal{L}_{\alpha} -GAN, a dual objective GAN that uses a function from this class for the generator and any canonical discriminator loss function that admits the same optimizer as VanillaGAN [1]. We show that under some regularity (convexity/concavity) conditions on \mathcal{L}_{\alpha}, the minimax game played with these two loss functions is equivalent to the minimization of a Jensen- f_{\alpha} -divergence, a Jensen-type divergence and another natural extension of the Jensen-Shannon divergence (in addition to the Jensen-Rényi divergence [6]), where the generating function f_{\alpha} of the divergence is computed directly from the CPE loss function \mathcal{L}_{\alpha}. This result recovers various prior dual-objective GAN equilibrium results, unifying them under one parameterized generator loss function. The newly obtained Jensen- f_{\alpha} -divergence, which belongs to the class of symmetric f -divergences with different generating functions (see Remark 1), is a useful measure of dissimilarity between distributions, as it requires a convex function f with a restricted domain given by the interval [0,2] (see Remark 2), in addition to its symmetry and finiteness properties.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we review f -divergence measures and introduce the Jensen- f -divergence as an extension of the Jensen-Shannon divergence. In Section 3, we establish our main result on the optimization of our unifying generator loss function (Theorem 1), and show that it applies to a large class of known GANs (Lemmas 2 - 4). In Section 4, we conduct experiments implementing different manifestations of \mathcal{L}_{\alpha} -GAN on three datasets, MNIST, CIFAR-10 and Stacked MNIST. Finally, we conclude the paper in Section 5.
